that situation and telling the story or opinion, and believing that opinion, we create that

have an emotional response to what we perceive. Well, one of the things we perceive is
the belief, the paradigm, according to which someone is causing us to feel this way. It’s
not really happening in any place other than our imagination, but we perceive that it’s
happening, even though what we perceive is something that we ourselves are creating.
So, we create this picture that someone is causing us to feel this way, we tell the story,
we believe the story, and we respond emotionally to that story that we’ve created. This is
how our own emotional state is created most of the time. And that’s largely the
realization and the shift in dynamics that started way back in the “Abdication of power”
exercise, that we should be continuing to practice.

As we’ve done the other exercises, hopefully we’ve become more aware of how we create
our own emotions: we create the story, we perceive the story we create, and then we
have an emotional response to what we perceive. Even if it’s just in our imagination, it’s
still perceived and our emotions respond as if it’s real. We can say that this is a self
hypnosis, where we’re hypnotizing ourselves into believing this paradigm, and then
respond emotionally to this paradigm as if it were true. It’s not a lot different than a
woman who has anorexia and who looks in the mirror. She doesn’t see what’s in the
mirror, but she sees what she imagines, and that’s that she’s overweight. She believes
she’s overweight and she responds to the paradigm that she sees, which is of being
                                                                                                                                   1/8

overweight. She can be all of seventy two pounds, but she’s living by and responding to
emotionally, and acting, according to what she sees in the paradigm, not what’s in the
mirror. We can say she has hypnotized herself into that reality. It’s actually not a reality.
She’s hypnotized herself into that perception. So for her it’s the reality, her personal
reality. I want that to be clear for us to see how we create our own perceptions. We
create them, we believe them, we respond emotionally to them. And understand this:
other people are doing the same thing, and they are not aware that they are doing it.

Understanding all this brings us to this exercise “False claims of power”, which is about
understanding that not only this is how we often create our own emotions, with our own
belief paradigms, but that it’s also how other people create their emotions with their
belief paradigms. And having understood this, we can see: “Ok, other people are
doing this. This is how they are responding to their own stories and their
own opinions, and it has more to do with how they see the world according
to their paradigms, and with how they hypnotize themselves, than with
anything we or the world are doing to them.” So we can see that other people are
operating their own dreams (you can call it “dreams” cause they are not realities) or
belief paradigms, and they are creating their own emotions largely within them. And
then, there comes the next step, which is that then they often blame other people or
circumstances for what’s causing their emotion. They might even blame us. They might
comment to us that the situation is really disappointing, or even say: “What you’ve done
has been disappointing to me,” or “You disappoint me.” But if someone is saying that we
disappoint him, when they say: “I’m disappointed with you,” that emotion that they’re
feeling is created within them, because they had an image of what they thought we
should do or should be, their Judge compared what we did with that image in their
imagination, we didn’t meet that expectation image that they had, and they felt a
victimization because we didn’t meet their standards. They then feel that emotion,
disappointment, and say we caused it. They did the whole thing in their head and they
say we caused it. And it’s understandable, they believe that.

The important part for us to realize is that if we are aware of how they create those
pictures in their head, how their Judge and the Victim interpret those images of
expectations and create their own emotion, based on those agreements about us, then
we can be very clear with ourselves that we did not cause or create their
disappointment. We are really not responsible for how they feel, because we couldn’t go
and rework those pictures in their imagination. If we could control those pictures in
their imagination, we could manage their expectations of us, and not just manage, but
control them. But the reality is that we may be able to influence them, but we can’t
control them. So, we are not responsible, and we don’t have power to change what goes
on in other people’s imagination. Yes, we can influence, but we can’t control. And if we
can’t control what people are doing in their mind, and the conclusions their Judge and
Victim are coming up with, we certainly can’t control the emotions they get as a result.
And if that’s the case, then they’re responsible for their emotional state, they are
responsible for creating the disappointment. And if they are angry with us, they are
responsible for creating the anger they have about us. This is what’s important to know.

                                                                                                                                   2/8

And more importantly, instead of just knowing it, it’s important to be aware of, to be
conscious of, to observe how people create their own emotions, and that they may use
you as a character, as a subject matter for their stories, but that you don’t actually create
their emotions.

Realizing it goes completely contrary to our upbringing. Our upbringing has taught
us that if someone is upset, if someone is disappointed, if we haven’t met someone’s
expectations, and they have an emotional reaction because of it, then we are indeed
responsible for how they feel, that we indeed have fault. And that elicits in us, invokes in
us guilt and shame for not being what they expect us to be. We feel like we’ve let them
down, or disappointed, or have done the wrong thing, while that isn’t what’s going on at
all. We actually feel the guilt and the shame because when they say something like: “You
really disappointed me,” we, in our mind, create an image of what we should have done,
we create an image that we are not this person that we should be, our Judge does the
comparison and says: “Yeah, I’m not that person I should be,” and our Victim takes that
assessment and says: “Oh, I’m not what I should be, I disappointed myself, I failed to
meet my expectations.” And the Victim accepts that judgment, and now we have the
guilt and the shame, and the unworthiness. We can say that they communicate those
images in the words that they share. And in the words we decode those words, putting
our own implied agreements about what the expectation was and what we are, if we are
not what we’re supposed to be, we take on those agreements and create the emotion.
This is a power of words. You could say, implied and embedded in that one sentence
“You disappointed me,” is the conveyance of those images of what we are supposed to
be, the conveyance of the image of this other image of ourselves as a failure, the
conveyance of how we should feel about ourselves, what judgments and victimization
we should make about ourselves for the failure to meet this expected image, and ending
up as the failure image. This is the mathematics, the creation, and the calculation that
goes on in the imagination in the mind. It can go on very fast in terms of that we can
create those images of what we’re supposed to be, and the image of the failure for not
being what we’re supposed to be, in a heart beat, or we can draw them up from things
on file in our memory, and so we can go to them rather quickly.

Anyhow, this is just to give you an idea of the details about what imagination is doing,
that creates within us this emotion of guilt and shame for having created an emotion in
someone else, when we did not actually do it. And, by the way, they didn’t make us feel
guilty. We did that with ourselves, with our own image creation and believing our own
images, and the Judge and the Victim story about not being that image that we are
supposed to be, that we’ve just created. We can’t say they made us feel guilty or
ashamed either, cause the truth is that we did that number on our own.

What I want us to be aware of in this assignment are those places, those interactions
where we assume responsibility for what other people are feeling. If we understand that
this is how we create our own emotions, and we understand this is how other people
create their own emotions too, then when people blame us or hold us responsible for
how they feel, as we have the awareness of how they really create their emotions, we do

                                                                                                                                   3/8

not have to accept the responsibility for how they feel, and therefore we do not have to
feel guilty or ashamed for their reaction, but we could say that what they are doing is
abdicating the power of their emotional state to us.

Now, it’s very tempting to take that responsibility over their emotions, because one of
the temptations is: “If I am responsible… If I really did make them feel this
way… Then I am more powerful,” and if I am powerful, then not only can I keep
them from feeling angry or disappointed, but I can also make them happy. And there’s
a sense of empowerment we play, when we take on that kind of power, which is to
say when we take on the responsibility for other people’s emotions. And it is not always
clear it has a down side. In our mind it’s like: “Ok, good, I can do something, I am
powerful here.” Well, we have to unhook from that temptation. We have to recognize
with awareness how they really create their own emotions, go to a little bit of humility
and say: “You know, I’m not that powerful. It’s just not within my power to
go invoke in other people’s emotions like that.” It’s a step down in power, as you
step up in awareness. Well, you can say it’s not really a step down in power, because you
never really had that power to begin with. What you’re really stepping down from is the
illusion that you had the power over their emotional state at all anyways. And once you
step out of that illusion, you are no longer subject to the guilt and the shame that come
with assuming responsibility for someone else’s emotional state. We don’t wanna be
responsible when we feel guilty or ashamed, but it’s very tempting to feel responsible
because of the seduction of power. So, when someone’s happy and they thank us, and
they attribute it to us – we need to be aware of that one also. We can say: “Hey, I’m
thrilled that you think so, but I don’t agree that I’m really responsible.” And maybe it’s
not appropriate to say that out loud, but at least in our own mind, in our own
awareness, let’s have that clarity.

I wanna talk about a couple of dynamics that we get into to help us identify when we are
assuming power over other people’s emotional state, that we don’t really have:

1) Any time that people are saying, “You make me feel this,” or “You really upset me,”
or “What your actions did create within me this emotion,” – those are big red flags and
you need to catch those words.

2) Other ways that you might find yourself taking responsibility for how other people
feel, is just what you’re doing in your imagination. Suppose we’re thinking to
ourselves: “Oh, if I do this, she will be really upset, this will really tick her off,” “If I
don’t do this, he will be upset with me.” What we’re doing right there in the story we’re
telling, without anybody else in the room, is that we’re assuming how someone will
react, and that our actions or inaction will create that emotion within them. Now, it’s
true that if we do something or don’t do something – that may trigger an agreement that
they have, in which they create their own emotions, based on that agreement. But that’s
a very different thing. Knowing and being aware that yes, we can do things that will
trigger other people’s emotions, and then refraining from doing these things – that’s
very different than taking responsibility for how people feel. So, much of this we’ll play
out in our imagination, in assuming how people will react. And when we assume how
                                                                                                                                   4/8

people will react, or when, based on our experience with people, we know darn well how
they’re gonna react, we may start to modify our behavior. We may try to go in and
appease them, and make them happy, and make them feel better. We may go over the
top, making sure they have everything that they ask for. The question we can start to
identify this with is “What archetype is that?” Is it the Hero that says: “Ok, I’m
gonna go cheer her up… I’m gonna go make him feel great”? Is it the Prostitute that goes
in, that says: “I’ve gotta do this for this person or else they’re gonna yell at me”? The
latter is a “Victim-Prostitute” dynamic, where people go and do a lot of work in order to
avoid somebody’s emotional poison. But they work to avoid that emotional poison,
because they have the agreements allowing it. If you have the awareness that it’s others’
emotional poison, and you don’t believe in their projection of you and in their
disappointment in you, you don’t feel that emotion. But if we are not aware, then in
order to avoid having that thrust upon us, we may go out of our way in hard work. That
could be an archetype of a Prostitute. I already talked about how the Judge will spin the
story in the mind, and how the Victim will spin the story in the mind. The Princess may
argue that she doesn’t deserve to be treated like that. And in the truth of our integrity, if
someone’s angry at us, pretty much that we don’t deserve to be treated like that. But the
Princess may use that and exaggerate that understanding as a reason to be upset and be
angry back. So, that then becomes a process where the Judge and the Victim exaggerate
that element of truth, that honest assessment, into an exaggeration and really indulge in
more emotional reaction of being angry back.

So, these are the responses of the archetypes that can help identify some of the follow on
behaviors, after you’ve already taken responsibility for how someone else feels, being
seduced by the power of that illusion that we actually have control over other people’s
emotional states.

There’s a clarity within this, that I wanna share, that happens as we become very
attuned to what emotions we feel. And this goes back to the “Emotions” exercise. When
someone is upset or sad, whether he blames us or not, as we care for him, or even if he’s
a complete stranger, we don’t like to see him being unhappy, angry or sad. And so,
there’s an instinctive part of our nature in that we take no joy in seeing someone in
unpleasant emotional state, seeing him emotionally suffering. When we see someone in
hardship, even someone we don’t know, and we can feel compassion for them. Not
necessarily sadness, but understanding that they are in an emotional pain. And this is
particularly the case with people we love and are close to. We take no pleasure and
enjoyment in seeing someone in pain (when we do take enjoyment in it, we need to be
looking at the Villain archetype in that, by the way). This is just intrinsic human nature
as a collective communal species. So, there is a place where when we do something, and
it ends up hurting someone emotionally, or hurting someone physically, there is a
genuine emotional response, and that feeling is remorse. There may be a situation
where we’re in the interaction and our pressure bursts, our anger comes out of our
mouth, and we share it with someone, maybe someone we love, and it hurts their
feelings and hits them emotionally, and now they really feel sad and guilty for what we
said or what we reminded them of in those words of anger. And when we see that they

                                                                                                                                   5/8

hurt, we then have an honest, intrinsic, authentic feeling of remorse for seeing someone
hurt, while we played a role in creating their pain. It doesn’t mean we are completely
responsible, but we’re partially responsible, there is an element of responsibility. Had
we not said those words, that wouldn’t have happened. So we’re responsible for what we
say, but they are responsible for what they hear and what they do with it. In that
interaction, when we see someone hurt by what we’ve done, there is the genuine feeling
of remorse. When we then say: “Oh, I shouldn’t have done that,” “I’m a terrible person
for having done that to them,” – that emotion is being elicited by the story of what we’ve
done and by the images we project in our mind of what we should have done and how
we should have been different, but we weren’t. Now, the remorse has gone into guilt
and shame, and those are not the same kind of authentic, intrinsic emotions. Those are
manufactured by story. Then, the honest remorse turns into indulgence through the
story of a lot more guilt and shame. In this way we could say guilt and shame are
artificially manufactured by the story, and remorse is authentic. Then there is a fine line
between the two, because often we see someone that we may have hurt or disappointed,
and maybe we weren’t able to keep our commitment, and they are disappointed, and we
see their pain, and there could be genuine remorse and sorrow. But when we start
creating the story about what we’ve done, and we believe the story, and we perceive the
story and then believe it, that perception creates a whole different series of emotions
that we’ll call indulgence. And that’s emotional suffering. The remorse is real. The
emotions of guilt and shame are real, but they artificially manufactured.

The area that I want you to put your attention on in the next few weeks is where you
take responsibility for other people’s emotions. When other people say: “You make me
feel this way,” how do you respond? What emotions come up for you? What behavior do
you then go into, and what archetype is running those behaviors? Where are the places
where you assume people are going to respond to you emotionally this way or that way,
and you go making the efforts to manage how they’re gonna feel emotionally? Or maybe
you go trying to make everything right, and you go feeling resentful, because they put all
that weight of their happiness on you, and you don’t wanna carry that burden, and then
yes, you can feel resentful, and you can go into a Saboteur kind of response, just to get
back at them for having that expectation of you.

These are different kinds of responses that we run in our imagination, and then play out
in our behavior, because we assume that how someone’s gonna react emotionally is
dependent on us. We have essentially assumed power over their emotional state. And
that’s false. That’s completely false. We do not have the power over their emotional
state. They may say we do, but it doesn’t mean we have to agree to their abdication of
power. Because they say we made them feel a certain way, doesn’t mean we did. Just the
same way that because we said someone made us feel a certain way, doesn’t mean that
they did it. Then, we need to be aware of: a) we are not responsible for their emotion; b)
we are not guilty for having them feel the way they feel; c) we are also not that powerful
force that can control other people’s emotional state, as tempting and as seductive as
that agreement is, and as much as we believe how life would be so great, if we could
control everybody else’s emotional state. Well, that’s our assumption of how life would

                                                                                                                                   6/8

be so great if we could. We have to let that go. We have to give up that false claim in our
mind that we’re that powerful. Yes, the truth is we’re extraordinarily powerful beings.
But so is everybody else. Everybody else has power, just like we do, to create with their
life, and it doesn’t mean they have power over other people’s emotional state. Yes, we
are powerful, and everybody else is equally powerful. We’re just not really powerful over
each other. We may be able to influence, but we can’t control.

So, keep you attention on what people say to you to try and hook you into believing
the false claims of power over their emotional state. Pay attention to what scenarios
you run in your imagination about how other people are gonna feel emotionally
about what you do or don’t do. And pay attention to your behaviors in terms of what
you are doing or refraining from doing, that maybe you wanna do, because you’re
concerned with how someone will react emotionally. Because underneath that
management of your actions is the assumption that you can control someone else’s
emotional state. And that’s just not true. That’s a completely false claim. And the other
place is to pay attention to what your actual actions and reactions are, to see
where you’re trying to manage their emotions.

The other element of this exercise that you can add to make it a little more interesting,
and heighten your awareness of this dynamic, is to watch very closely how other
people deal with power over their emotional state, and how they assume
that they have power over other people’s emotional state. The more you can
watch other people in how they abdicate power over their emotional state, or how they
assume falsely responsibility over other people’s emotional state, and the reactions they
go into, trying to manage other people’s reactions, the more you will become aware of
your dynamics around this issue.

As your awareness grows, and you are able to let go of this seductive illusion of power
over other people’s emotions, you will find yourself less and less guilty, less and less
ashamed, less and less unworthy, less and less disappointed in yourself. All this because
you’ll find yourself less and less trying to live by other people’s expectations. You’ll
realize and will be more aware of that you’re not responsible for other people’s
expectations of you, that that’s their own creation in their own mind, in their own
imagination, and that it’s not up to you to live up to them. Now, they might trying to
motivate you in that reaction, based on their judgement or reactions, which is
essentially the game of punishment and reward that they play, trying to get you to be
what they want.

And let me put in here just a little warning: when you watch people do this dynamic and
maybe try to hook you, guilt you, or be angry with you, and you take less and less
responsibility for it, my suggestion is not to point out to them what they’re doing,
because particularly in that moment they have no interest in learning about themselves,
but they have more interest in understanding why you are doing what you’re doing or
not doing what they want you to do. In those moments – that’s their interest and that’s
their focus. It may be possible later to share with them your point of view about it, about
how you’re looking at it differently these days, but certainly not when their emotions are
                                                                                                                                   7/8

charged up. That’s not time to talk to them about this. And there may not be a time to
talk to them at all, because for them to understand what you’re saying, they have to
completely rewire and change it to the different paradigm about who’s creating their
own emotional state, and they may not wanna do that. So it may be healthier in the
relationship to not point it out. You’re gonna have to make that as your own judgment
call. And every situation is different.

Ok, I’ve started to bring together a lot of different elements here: the abdication of
power, the emotions, the projections that our Victim and Judge make in our mind,
bringing this into communication with other people, how not to believe other people,
because their opinion of us is based on their projection of us in their mind, and on how
they create their emotions. There is a lot of elements to this, and to keep it all in your
awareness is no small feat. As you practice more and more, and you’re able to keep
more and more in your awareness of these different dynamics going on in other people’s
imagination, their emotional body and your imagination, your emotional body, it
becomes quite an amazing show.

Scientists study the brain and they say something to the effect that the mind is very
powerful, and we only really use 10 or 15% or it. I don’t really think that’s true. I just
don’t think they’ve noticed what’s going on with the other 90%.

So, good luck with the exercise. Awareness. Let go of this seduction of power. Refrain
from believing someone else’s story about how you’re creating their emotions and have
a great day. Thank you.





                                                                                                                                   8/8

Pathway to Happiness
   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/12-illusions-of-power
                                                                         May 10, 2019



12 Illusions of Power

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/InsZX30nr5Y

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Illusions of Power lesson audio
You may want to listen multiple times.

2. Pay attention to your thoughts and words. Notice when you think, state, or feel
responsible for others emotions. Re-frame your thoughts and beliefs to acknowledge
their responsibility for their own emotions. This can free you from a misplaced burden.

3. Pay attention to when others claim you are the one responsible for their
emotions. They are making an abdication of power claim, and with awareness you can
perceive it as false. It doesn’t mean you should counter them. They won’t have the
same perception of how emotions are created so getting in a debate or argument may
not be worth it.

Some notes

We have extraordinary power.
We just don’t have it over other people all the time for everything they feel. It might
seem that we do because people react to us, but its not that simple. People have
agreements. We say or do things that activate their “buttons” of agreements, and then
they react in a manner accordance to their own agreements. These “buttons” are pre-
programmed emotions of their characters lying in wait. Looks like we have the power,
but we don’t. The moment they change their agreements/beliefs, we have nothing to
activate. Or at least we don’t activate them the same way. They change their beliefs,
and what they do changes. We can say the same thing but they don’t respond in the
same way.





                                                                                                                                           1/5

So, this bears the question, how much responsibility should we take for other peoples
emotions?

Being aware of this chain of events that makes up an emotional reaction gives us other
avenues for understanding responsibility and control. It can reduce layers of guilt, and
shame about “saying something wrong.”

This awareness can lessen the self judgment story about “having done something
wrong to upset them.” Then your Victim character has less to feel guilt or shame
about.

Without that false responsibility, your Caretaker, Pleaser, Prostitute, and Hero
characters, who have been trying to manage other peoples emotions can relax. They
don’t have to control and fix things, because they can’t. It is not in your characters
power to control other people’s characters.

After you let dynamics like this go, you can begin to be curious about what you will do
with all the free time, energy, and attention you will have freed up. We cover that in the
Self Mastery Course II.

Resistance to change
At this point in the process there is likely less and less resistance. You also have the
exercises to address it. You can use those tools to identify how the various characters
respond to an exercise. What their fears, objections, and logic they come up with for not
doing a practice. You can also apply skepticism to various characters say, and find
holes in their logic.

The “hole” might be a half truth. There is something truthful about what they are saying,
but they are leaving something out as well.

In this case the common objection is that we do have responsibility over how others
feel. What we can affect others emotions. Fair enough. This is true. The false part is
that we are not solely responsible. They have some share of responsibility for their
emotions. Figuring out what percentage is a bit difficult.

If I am a close relative to you, and I get angry at you, you are likely to respond with fear.
We are going to have more emotional responses to people we are close with. This can
be amplified by the fact that I am 6’3″ and about 200 lbs and I might be bigger
physically. Having a fearful response is understandable. I created the circumstances for
a fearful response. I am in part responsible for your fear. Or, if you have known me for a
long time, you know I am not a dangerous person, and so you might find it funny that I
got so angry about something. Did I make you laugh by being so angry? Yes you had a
response, and I was the stimulus.

However, if you left the toilet seat up, or a glass in the living room, and I get angry at


                                                                                                                                    2/5

you….. you didn’t cause that anger. I am responsible for upsetting myself with my belief
about toilet seats and dirty dishes. You did a kind of harmless act that didn’t warrant
anger on my part. I might be upset and blame you for my anger, but you would know
that I am lying. I might believe the lie, and feel it as truth, but it is still a lie.

You might have a fearful response, but you don’t need to go to guilt, shame, or any
sense of responsibility for my anger and upset. These are separate emotions.

I am largely responsible for the fear response you are having. Yes, I can affect your
emotions. If someone makes such a strong expression to you, under certain
circumstances, you will have a response. You might respond with fear, or anger, or
freeze because your fight or flight system got triggered. Much of it depends on the
environment you are in and your history of programmed responses.

Maybe the fear is a real response to the present moment. Perhaps the anger to defend
your self when threatened is a real response. Or anger and freeze response is there
from a repressed emotion, or past event being triggered.

In this scenario, it is difficult to draw a clear line. Each circumstance will take the
inventory of two people to unwind and see who is responsible for the different emotions.
One breakdown might look like this:

I reacted and generated anger because of a belief I have about dirty dishes. I let it out
with a whole lot of repressed emotion that had been building for 12 years. It wasn’t the
water glass or you leaving it there that created the anger.

Your fear, was a natural response to my anger. In a way, I created that circumstance,
and your fear was a natural authentic response. I created the circumstance and so that
is largely my creation, with some responsibility from you. How much is hard to say. We
could say that I initiated your fear. But that doesn’t mean that you “made me angry” by
leaving the water glass on the counter.

Then if you added your own anger, or panic freeze response, then that is largely your
responsibility. My part is responsibility for pushing that program button. I am responsible
for pushing that program, but you are responsible for having that program to be
pushed.

Overall, it’s a mess. And maybe we don’t get the exact amount of responsibility
allocated in just the right places. Largely because you can’t know for sure. But we are
getting a lot closer to the truth. Each time you remove a layer of false beliefs the
emotions become less and less. Then the next layer gets easier to remove.

In this mess, the assignment is about letting others be responsible for their
emotions as much as possible.

We are eliminating a lot of the judge and victim layers that interfere with taking proper
responsibility for our part, and that interferes with others taking responsibility for theirs.

                                                                                                                                    3/5

Figuring out responsibility, and what caused which emotion, is a more involved
inventory process. It’s not the kind of thing to leave to the snap judgments of your
characters.

Finding proper responsibility for the emotions is not about finding fault. Finding
responsibility is only helpful because it helps hunt down repressed emotions to be
released, and false beliefs to be identified and dismantled.

One of the things you might resist is the “work” of doing this kind of inventory math. But
consider this, if you don’t get it sorted out closer to the truth, then you will still be doing
the work of living in the emotional reactions of lies.

Common questions
